solution:
Correct. The temperature range helps the wind in its work.
The work of the wind is most prominent in deserts and semi-arid regions, and the chapter says that mechanical weathering occurs on a large scale in these regions, so powdered rock and sand spread over a large area. This loose sand is the material the wind picks up and carries, and the sand particles striking the rocks are what cause erosion. Without such breaking up of rock there would be nothing for the wind to work with.
[Note: the chapter explains the large-scale mechanical weathering of desert regions but does not itself use the words 'temperature range'.]

Incorrect. The correct statement is: Wind's work is more prominent than other agents of erosion in desert regions.
The chapter states that the erosional, transportational and depositional work of the wind is more prominent in deserts and semi-arid regions. There is hardly any obstacle to the wind there, and plenty of loose sand is available, so the wind and not the river is the chief agent in a desert.

Incorrect. The correct statement is: The work of groundwater is effective in areas with soluble rocks such as limestone.
Rainwater seeps below the surface through porous rocks or through cracks in the rocks. The soluble minerals in these rocks get dissolved in the water and are carried away with the groundwater, and this dissolving is the erosional work of the groundwater. Landforms such as sinkholes, limestone caves, stalactites and stalagmites are therefore formed in limestone areas, not simply wherever the rock happens to be soft.

Correct. The work of wind is not limited like river, glacier or the sea waves and takes place everywhere.
A river can work only along the channel in which it flows, a glacier only where temperatures stay below freezing point and snow accumulates, and the sea waves only along the coast. The wind, being a gaseous agent, blows over the land surface and, as the chapter says, there is hardly any obstacle in its transportational work. Its work is nevertheless most prominent in deserts and semi-arid regions, where loose sand is easily available.

Incorrect. The correct statement is: The ice in the middle of the glacier moves faster than the ice at its base and at its sides.
The glacier rubs against its bed and its banks, which is why it erodes them on a large scale; this friction holds back the ice that touches them. The chapter also says that at the base of the layer the snow starts melting because of the friction and the pressure of the layers above. The ice away from the bed and the banks meets no such resistance, so it moves fastest.
[Note: the chapter does not directly compare the speed of the ice at the side of a glacier with the speed of the ice at its base.]

Correct. No change is needed.
As the steepness of the slope decreases, the transporting capacity of the river reduces and it begins to flow slowly. The sediments it has been carrying then settle in its bed and on its banks. This is how landforms such as alluvial fans, flood levees, flood plains and deltas are formed.

Correct. No change is needed.
A river originates at a much higher altitude than the sea level and there it flows at a great speed, which is why its power to erode is great. A glacier, on the other hand, moves slowly along the slope; the chapter notes that glaciers move only about 1 cm to 1 m a day. So a river does flow much faster than a glacier, though the glacier still erodes on a large scale because the mass of its ice is so great.

Incorrect. The correct statement is: The speed of the glacier is more in the middle than at both its banks.
The glacier rubs against its two banks and its bed as it moves, and the chapter says it erodes its own banks and its bed on a large scale. This friction slows down the ice touching the banks, while the ice in the middle of the glacier is free to move and therefore moves fastest.
[Note: the chapter describes the erosion of the banks and the bed by the glacier but does not state the middle-and-banks speed difference in so many words.]

The wrong pair is (1) Deposition - V-shaped valley.
A V-shaped valley is not formed by deposition at all. The chapter lists it under the erosional work of rivers: near its source the river flows at great speed, its riverbed and banks are worn away, and gorges (canyons), V-shaped valleys and waterfalls are formed. The correct pair would therefore be Erosion - V-shaped valley.
Pair (3) Erosion - Mushroom Rocks is correct, since the chapter lists mushroom rocks among the landforms produced by the erosional work of the wind. Pair (2) Transport - Ripple Marks is acceptable in the sense that ripple marks are made of sand that the wind has carried, but note that the chapter itself places ripple marks under the depositional work of the wind, along with sand dunes, barchans, seifs and loess plains.

All three diagrams show landforms made by a river.
(1) The first diagram shows a wide valley cut down into the rock in the shape of the letter V, with the water flowing at its bottom. It is a V-shaped valley, formed by the erosional work of the river in its upper course.
(2) The second diagram shows a very narrow and very deep cut in the rock, with steep, almost vertical sides and a thin stream at the bottom. It is a gorge (canyon), also formed by the erosional work of the river where it flows fast through hard rock.
(3) The third diagram is seen from above. The river comes in from one side, and near its mouth it splits into several branches, with triangular masses of sediment settled between them. It is a delta, formed by the depositional work of the river, because near the sea the riverbed becomes very wide and the speed of the water becomes very slow, so the sediments get deposited.

| Rivers | Wind | Glacier | Sea Waves | Groundwater |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| waterfall, delta, pothole | barchans, mushroom rock | cirque, arête, moraine | beach, lagoons | sinkholes, pillars |

Waterfalls are cut by the fast-flowing river and deltas are built by it where it meets the sea. Barchans are sand dunes deposited by the wind and mushroom rocks are carved by the sand it carries. Cirques and arêtes are eroded by the glacier, and moraines are the sediments the glacier carries and deposits. Beaches and lagoons are made by the depositional work of the sea waves. Sinkholes are formed by groundwater in limestone areas.
[Note: the chapter does not name potholes or pillars anywhere in its text. They have been placed under rivers and groundwater because a pothole is a hollow ground out in a riverbed and a pillar is formed underground where a stalactite and a stalagmite meet, but the chapter itself gives no support for either.]

Gorges (canyons), V-shaped valleys and waterfalls are the landforms formed by the erosional work of the rivers.
A river begins at a much higher altitude than the sea level, so there it flows at a great speed and its power to erode is great. The riverbed and the river banks are worn away by the fast flow of water and by the sand particles and pebbles carried in it, and by the tributaries that join the main river. These landforms are therefore found in the upper, hilly course of a river.

Groundwater is responsible for the formation of stalactites and stalagmites. They are formed inside limestone caves under the ground.
Rainwater seeps below the surface through porous rocks and cracks, and the soluble minerals of the rock dissolve in it and flow along with the groundwater. When this groundwater evaporates, or when the amount of dissolved minerals becomes more than the water can hold, the dissolved material begins to settle. This deposition builds up stalactites and stalagmites, along with sinkholes and limestone caves.

Beaches, sand bars and lagoons are the landforms produced by the depositional work of the sea waves.
The material eroded from the coast collects on the sea bed. Because of the tides it keeps moving towards the coast and away from it, and it becomes fine by attrition as the pieces strike one another. This fine material is laid down at places where the effect of the waves is less, and there these landforms are built up.
The sediments carried by a glacier are called moraines. Depending on where they are deposited, moraines are of four types: ground moraines, lateral moraines, medial moraines and terminal moraines.

The picture shows one long slope running from high snowy mountains down to the seacoast, and the landforms of four different agents can be seen on it, one after the other.
Work of glaciers (in the high mountains): sharp, pointed snow-covered peaks (horns) with knife-edged ridges (arêtes) between them, bowl-shaped hollows filled with snow at the heads of the ice (cirques), long tongues of ice moving down the valleys with dark bands of moraine along them, and the broad U-shaped valleys they have carved out.
Work of the wind (in the dry, sandy tract beyond the mountains): rows of long, curved sand dunes (barchans and seifs) lying across the yellow desert surface.
Work of rivers (from the mountains to the sea): narrow, deep valleys and gorges high up where the streams flow fast; then, on the green plain, a river swinging from side to side in wide bends (meanders) across its flood plain; and finally, at its mouth, a fan-shaped delta where the river splits into several branches and drops its sediment into the sea.
Work of sea waves (along the coast): steep sea cliffs standing above the water, isolated pillars of rock left standing in the sea in front of them (sea stacks) with a wave-cut platform at their foot, a long sandy beach, and a sand bar built across a bay with a lagoon of quiet water behind it.
The smoking cone rising above the mountains is a volcano. It is not the work of any agent of erosion; it is made by forces working inside the earth.
[Note: no landform of groundwater, such as a sinkhole or a limestone cave, can be seen in the picture, since these are formed under the ground.]
